cards.front: Define the current account. Evaluate whether a depreciation of the pound will improve the UK's current account and raise growth.
cards.back:
Current account — the part of the balance of payments that records trade in goods and services, plus income such as profits and interest earned abroad and transfers such as foreign aid.

For: UK exports get cheaper abroad and imports dearer → export sales rise and imports fall → the current account improves → net exports raise aggregate demand → higher real GDP and more jobs.

It depends on:

  • The Marshall-Lerner condition: if the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports add up to less than 1, the current account gets worse.
  • Time (the J-curve): demand is inelastic at first, so the trade balance worsens before it improves.
  • Spare capacity: with unemployed workers and idle factories, firms can raise output, so growth and jobs gain most. Near full capacity, the extra demand mainly raises prices.
  • Import content of exports: many UK exports use imported parts. Their costs rise with the depreciation, so part of the price advantage is lost.

Judgement: a weaker pound can improve the current account and raise growth, but only after a lag and only if demand is elastic enough. If the economy is near full capacity, the main result may be inflation.

source.verbatim: the part of the balance of payments that records trade in goods and services, plus income such as profits and interest earned abroad and transfers such as foreign aid.

cards.front: Define the Eurozone. Build the chains of reasoning: what does the euro bring firms and countries inside it, and what does sharing one monetary policy cost them?
cards.back:
Eurozone — the group of EU countries that use the euro as their currency, with interest rates set for all of them by the European Central Bank (ECB).

Benefits:

  • No exchange rate risk: a Spanish firm selling to Italy is paid in euros → its revenue cannot be hit by a currency change, and it pays nothing to convert money → lower costs and easier planning → more trade between members.
  • Clear prices: prices across the Eurozone are in one currency → buyers compare them easily → firms face more competition → lower prices for consumers.
  • More investment: a firm from outside, such as a Japanese electronics maker, can build one factory and sell across the Eurozone without currency risk → more FDI into member countries.

Costs:

  • One interest rate for all: the ECB sets a single rate → it may be too high for a member in recession and too low for one with rising inflation → each country loses a tool to manage its own economy.
  • No exchange rate to adjust: a member whose costs rise faster than its neighbours' cannot let its currency fall → its exports stay expensive → it can regain competitiveness only by cutting wages and prices, which means higher unemployment for years.

It depends on how closely the country's economy moves with the rest, and how easily workers and money move to where the jobs are. The UK never joined, so UK firms trading with the Eurozone still face changes in the pound-euro rate.

source.verbatim: the group of EU countries that use the euro as their currency, with interest rates set for all of them by the European Central Bank (ECB).

cards.front: Define a push factor, a pull factor and a saturated market. Build the chains for the two push factors.
cards.back:
Push factor — a problem in the home market that drives a firm to look for sales abroad.

Pull factor — a benefit of selling abroad that attracts a firm to expand there.

Saturated market — a market where most people who want the product already have it, so sales grow slowly and come mainly from replacements.

The two push factors:

  • A saturated home market: few new customers → sales and revenue stop growing → the firm sells in countries where demand is still rising → higher sales and profit.
  • Competition: more rivals at home → price cuts to keep customers → lower margins and profit → the firm sells where it faces less competition and can charge more.

Nearly every UK home already has a washing machine, so a maker can only grow at home by taking customers from rivals. Where ownership is still rising, every new buyer is extra demand.

The two pull factors are economies of scale and risk spreading.

source.verbatim: a problem in the home market that drives a firm to look for sales abroad.

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning for the two pull factors. When does risk spreading work least well?
cards.back:
• Economies of scale: new export markets → higher output → bulk buying, and design and advertising costs spread over more units → lower average cost → lower prices or higher profit per unit.
  • Risk spreading: a recession hits the UK → UK sales fall, but sales in other countries hold up → revenue and cash flow stay steadier → less risk of losses and job cuts.

Risk spreading works best when the markets don't move together. Economies are more interdependent than they used to be, so a global recession can hit every market at once.

cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how can selling abroad extend a product's life cycle and raise capacity utilisation? What limits how much it helps?
cards.back:
• Extending the product life cycle: UK sales start to fall → the firm launches the product in a country where it is new → sales grow again → more revenue from a product whose development is already paid for → cash to fund new products.
  • Raising capacity utilisation: export orders → higher output from the same factory → fixed costs spread over more units → lower average cost and higher profit.

Selling in a new market is an extension strategy: it starts the life cycle again. It works when the product is new to customers abroad. A product replaced by better technology is likely to decline everywhere.

Exports can also fill a seasonal gap. A UK maker of winter coats is quiet in the British summer, when it is winter in New Zealand.

How much it helps depends on:

  • The cost of entering the market: marketing, shipping and adapting the product for a new country can cost more than the extra sales bring in.
  • Exchange rates: a stronger pound makes UK exports dearer abroad and cuts the value of foreign sales in pounds.
  • How much spare capacity there is: a firm already near full capacity would need a new factory to meet foreign orders, which removes the cost advantage.

cards.front:
Define offshoring and outsourcing. Is each of these offshoring, outsourcing or both?

  • (a) A UK toy firm pays a factory in China to make its toys.
  • (b) A UK insurer moves its claims team to its own office in South Africa.
  • (c) A UK hotel chain pays a local firm to run its laundry.
cards.back:
Offshoring — moving part of a firm's production or services to another country.

Outsourcing — paying another firm to carry out work the business used to do itself.

Offshoring is about where; outsourcing is about who. Offshoring moves work to another country. Outsourcing hands it to another firm, which may be in the same town.

  • (a) Both: the work moves abroad and to another firm.
  • (b) Offshoring only: the work moves abroad, but the insurer still does it itself.
  • (c) Outsourcing only: another firm does the work, but it stays in the UK.

In an extract, check which one the firm has done, or whether it has done both, and use the right term.

source.verbatim: moving part of a firm's production or services to another country.

cards.front: Evaluate whether a UK firm gains from offshoring or outsourcing its production, and who loses.
cards.back:
For:

  • Lower costs: when the work moves abroad, wages and rents are lower → lower unit costs → the firm can cut prices or earn a higher margin.
  • Focus: a specialist supplier does the routine work → the firm puts its staff and money into what it does best, such as design → a stronger product.

Against, for UK workers: jobs move abroad → staff are made redundant → lower incomes in the areas the work left.

It depends on:

  • Control over quality: it is harder to check work done by another firm thousands of miles away. Faults or poor working conditions at a supplier can damage the brand.
  • The length of the supply chain: goods take weeks to ship, so the firm reacts more slowly to changes in demand, and a blocked port can halt supplies.
  • Whether the cost gap lasts: as wages rise in emerging economies, the saving shrinks, and some firms bring work back home.

Judgement: it pays most where the work is routine, its quality is easy to check and demand changes little, and while the wage gap lasts. It pays least for a firm whose brand rests on quality, or which must react quickly to what customers want.

cards.front: Define disposable income. Why does a firm choosing a market to sell in look at both its level and its growth? Name the other four factors it weighs up.
cards.back:
Disposable income — household income after income tax and National Insurance, plus any state benefits. It is what people have to spend.

  • The level shows how many people can buy the product today.
  • The growth shows how the market will change. A country where average incomes are far below the UK's, but rising quickly, can be a better long-term prospect than a wealthy but saturated market.

Incomes rise → more households join the middle class → demand for income-elastic goods, such as cars, eating out and foreign holidays, grows faster than incomes → higher sales for firms that got in early.

The other four factors:

  • Ease of doing business: simple rules, quick approvals and little corruption.
  • Infrastructure: good roads, ports, power and internet access, so goods reach customers cheaply and on time, and online sales are possible.
  • Political stability: a steady government and laws that don't change suddenly.
  • Exchange rate: a stable rate, and a pound that isn't strong against the local currency.

source.verbatim: household income after income tax and National Insurance, plus any state benefits. It is what people have to spend.

cards.front: Define ease of doing business. Build the chains: how do red tape and political instability make a country a less attractive market?
cards.back:
Ease of doing business — how simple, quick and cheap it is to set up and run a firm in a country, from registering the company and getting permits to paying tax and enforcing contracts.

  • Red tape and corruption: months of delay and extra fees before trading starts → higher costs and later revenue → a lower return on the expansion.
  • Political instability: war, unrest or a sudden change of government → shops close, imports stop or the firm's assets are taken → lost sales and assets.

The World Bank used to rank countries on ease of doing business. It stopped in 2021 after finding problems with its data, so treat older rankings with care.

source.verbatim: how simple, quick and cheap it is to set up and run a firm in a country, from registering the company and getting permits to paying tax and enforcing contracts.

cards.front: Define the exchange rate. A UK firm sells in India. Build the chains: how does a stronger pound against the rupee affect its sales and its revenue in pounds?
cards.back:
Exchange rate — the price of one currency in terms of another.

  • Sales: UK goods cost more in rupees → customers buy fewer → lower sales.
  • Revenue in pounds: revenue earned in rupees converts into fewer pounds → lower revenue and profit in pounds.

If £1 rises from 100 to 110 rupees, a £50 jacket goes from 5,000 to 5,500 rupees. And 5.5 million rupees of sales, worth £55,000 at the old rate, are worth only £50,000 at the new one.

A weaker pound does the reverse. A rate that swings a lot makes planning hard, because the firm cannot tell what its foreign sales will be worth.

source.verbatim: the price of one currency in terms of another

cards.front: Name the nine factors that influence where a firm locates production. Why do three of them matter more for a production site than for a market to sell in?
cards.back:
Selling into a market asks: are there enough customers who can afford the product? Locating production asks: can the firm make the product there cheaply and reliably?

  • Costs of production: low wages, rents, energy and material costs cut unit costs, if productivity is high enough.
  • Skills and availability of labour: enough workers with the right skills. A shortage pushes wages up, and complex products need trained engineers.
  • Infrastructure: ports, roads and a reliable power supply, so materials arrive and goods leave on time.
  • Location in a trade bloc: a site inside the bloc the firm sells to pays no external tariff on goods sold in the bloc.
  • Government incentives: grants, tax breaks or cheap land cut the cost of building and running the site.
  • Ease of doing business: quick planning approval and simple rules, so the site opens sooner and costs less to run.
  • Political stability: a low risk of conflict or of the site being seized.
  • Natural resources: raw materials or cheap energy close by cut transport and energy costs. A quarry has to go where the stone is.
  • Likely return on investment: the highest expected profit for the money spent, which brings all the other factors together.

Infrastructure, ease of doing business and political stability are on both lists. They matter more for a production site, because the firm has put money into buildings and machinery it cannot easily move.

cards.front:
Define return on investment (ROI). A firm is choosing between two factory sites:

  • Site A costs £15 million and is expected to earn £1.8 million a year.
  • Site B costs £24 million and is expected to earn £2.4 million a year.

Calculate the ROI of each. Which is better value, and what could change the decision?
cards.back:
Return on investment (ROI) — the profit an investment earns as a percentage of its cost.

  • Site A: 1.8 ÷ 15 × 100 = 12%.
  • Site B: 2.4 ÷ 24 × 100 = 10%.

Site A is better value. Site B earns more profit in total, but less for each pound spent.

Unless Site A is riskier: a less stable country has to offer a higher expected ROI to be worth the risk.

source.verbatim: the profit an investment earns as a percentage of its cost

cards.front: Evaluate the factors a UK firm should weigh up when choosing a country in which to locate production.
cards.back:
No country scores well on everything, so the firm trades one factor off against another. The likely return on investment brings them together.

It depends on:

  • What the firm makes: shoes and simple assembly need lots of labour, so low wages count most. Aircraft parts need skilled staff and reliable power.
  • Productivity, not just wages: low wages cut unit costs only if productivity is high enough.
  • Where it sells: a site inside the trade bloc it sells to avoids the external tariff.
  • Risk against return: a less stable country has to offer a higher expected ROI to be worth the risk, because buildings and machinery cannot easily be moved.

Match the factor to the decision. Low wages are a reason to produce in a country, not to sell there, as they usually mean low disposable incomes.

Judgement: for a product that needs lots of labour, low wages decide it, as long as productivity and infrastructure are good enough. For a complex product, skills, reliable power and stability come first. In both cases the best site is the one with the highest expected ROI once the risk is allowed for.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Define glocalisation. How does it differ from globalisation as a way of selling worldwide?
cards.back:
Glocalisation — selling a global brand, but adapting the product or its marketing to suit the tastes and customs of each local market.

Globalisation, as a way of selling, is the other option: the firm treats the world as one market, with one product, one brand and one advertising campaign.

A global ice-cream brand keeps the same name and logo everywhere, but sells different flavours in each country to suit local tastes. That is glocalisation. Selling the same flavours everywhere, with the same adverts, would be globalisation.

Glocalisation is the geocentric approach to global markets. The wider meaning of globalisation, for the world economy, is in unit 2.4.1.

source.verbatim: selling a global brand, but adapting the product or its marketing to suit the tastes and customs of each local market.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Define the ethnocentric, geocentric and polycentric approaches to global markets, with the other name for each. Give each one's main advantage and disadvantage.
cards.back:
Ethnocentric approach — the domestic approach. The firm sells the same product abroad, in the same way, as it does at home.

Geocentric approach — the mixed approach. The firm treats the world as one market but adapts the product or marketing where local differences make it worthwhile. This is glocalisation.

Polycentric approach — the international approach. The firm treats each country as a separate market, with its own products and marketing, often run by local managers.

  • Ethnocentric: the cheapest, with no new products and the most economies of scale. But it ignores local tastes, so sales abroad can be low.
  • Geocentric: keeps most economies of scale while fitting local tastes. But it is hard to judge what to change, and head office and local managers can disagree.
  • Polycentric: the best fit with local tastes, so higher local sales. But it is the most expensive, with few economies of scale across markets, and the brand can look different in every country.

Geocentric and polycentric are easy to mix up. A geocentric firm has one global brand, changed only where it pays. A polycentric firm has a separate plan for every country.

A small exporter often starts with an ethnocentric approach, the cheapest way to begin selling abroad.

source.verbatim: the domestic approach. The firm sells the same product abroad, in the same way, as it does at home.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how might a UK firm adapt its price, promotion and place when it enters a new market abroad? What decides whether it should compete on price?
cards.back:
• Price: average incomes are lower than in the UK → the UK price would put the product out of reach → a lower local price, or a smaller pack at a lower price → more buyers, at a lower margin per unit.
  • Promotion: adverts use the local language, local faces and local media → customers relate to the brand → demand rises.
  • Place: the firm sells through the channels local buyers use, such as small local stores in one country and online in another → the product reaches more customers.

A UK shampoo maker might sell single-use sachets where incomes are low, rather than its full-size bottle.

Whether to compete on price depends on:

  • Local rivals' costs: local firms pay local wages and no shipping, so they can often undercut an importer. The importer may do better competing on brand and quality.
  • Price elasticity of demand: where buyers have low incomes and plenty of substitutes, demand is price elastic, so a high price loses many sales.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Define a brand. Build the chains: how can a well-known brand help a firm entering a new market abroad, and how can it hurt? What limits how much it helps?
cards.back:
Brand — a name, logo or design that identifies a firm's products and sets them apart from rivals'.

  • Recognition: customers already know the brand → they trust it and are willing to try it → less spent persuading them → faster sales growth.
  • Premium price: brand loyalty → demand becomes more price inelastic → the firm can charge more than local rivals → higher margins.
  • Risk to every market: a scandal or faulty product in one country is shared worldwide on social media → customers everywhere lose trust → sales fall in every market at once.

How much the brand helps depends on:

  • The strength of local brands: local firms may be more trusted and know local tastes better, so the global firm has to differentiate on something local customers value.
  • Whether the brand's image travels: a brand built on being British may appeal abroad or mean nothing, and a name or slogan can carry an unintended meaning.

source.verbatim: a name, logo or design that identifies a firm's products and sets them apart from rivals'.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Evaluate whether a firm selling worldwide should adapt its product to each market (glocalisation) or sell one standard product everywhere (globalisation).
cards.back:
For adapting: a product that fits local tastes → more local customers want it → higher sales and market share than a standard product would win.

For one standard product: one product made in large numbers → economies of scale in production and advertising → lower average cost → lower prices or higher margins in every market.

The cost of adapting: a different version for each market → extra market research and design, and shorter production runs → higher average cost and lower margins.

It depends on:

  • How much tastes differ: food, drink and clothing are tied to culture, so they usually need adapting. A calculator does the same job everywhere and sells almost unchanged.
  • The size of the market: adapting pays only if the extra sales cover the extra cost. A very large market can justify its own version; a small one may not.

Judgement: adapt where tastes differ a lot and the market is big enough for the extra sales to cover the extra cost. Otherwise one standard product, with its lower costs, is likely to earn more. Glocalising need not mean changing everything: a firm that keeps one global brand and adapts only where it pays keeps most of its economies of scale while fitting local tastes.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Define a demand-side factor and culture. How can culture and tastes affect demand for a UK product abroad?
cards.back:
Demand-side factor — anything about the customers in a market, such as their culture, tastes or language, that affects how much of a product they want to buy.

Culture — the shared beliefs, customs and way of life of a group of people.

  • Culture shapes what people buy and how they expect it to be sold. Religion affects diet, and it affects what an advert can show, from alcohol to how people dress.
  • Tastes differ even between similar countries: how sweet, salty or spicy food should be, portion sizes and favourite flavours.

A UK maker of sweet breakfast cereal may find it sells poorly in a country where people prefer a savoury breakfast.

So a product that sells well in the UK can fail abroad, because customers there want something different, or read its marketing differently.

source.verbatim: anything about the customers in a market, such as their culture, tastes or language, that affects how much of a product they want to buy.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: what happens when a firm ignores cultural and social factors in a market abroad? How can it cut the risk?
cards.back:
• The product misses: it does not suit local tastes or breaks a local custom → few customers buy it → low sales → the cost of entering the market is never recovered.
  • The brand suffers: an advert or pack offends local customers → complaints spread on social media → the brand's image is damaged → lower sales in that market, and possibly in others.

Cutting the risk: market research in each country, testing names, flavours and adverts on local customers before launch. Many firms also hire local staff or agents who know the market.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Explain how language, unintended meanings and inappropriate or inaccurate translations can hurt a firm selling abroad. Build the chains for sales and for legal and safety risks.
cards.back:
• Language: labels, packaging, websites, adverts and customer service all need to work in the local language. A country with more than one official language may need two or three on a single pack.
  • Unintended meanings: a brand name chosen in English can sound like a rude or silly word in another language. A hand gesture, colour or image that is friendly in the UK can mean something quite different elsewhere.
  • Inaccurate translations: a slogan translated word for word can lose its meaning, because jokes and sayings rarely carry across. Instructions or ingredients translated wrongly are worse, as customers may use the product unsafely.

The chains:

  • Sales: a name or slogan is confusing or laughable → customers don't take the product seriously → lower sales, plus the cost of new packaging and adverts to relaunch it.
  • Legal and safety risks: a label is translated wrongly → it breaks local labelling law or misleads customers → fines, product recalls and a damaged brand.

Cutting the risk: use native speakers to translate, and test names and adverts on local customers before launch.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Define a mass market and a niche market. When a UK firm sells abroad, how far does each type of firm adapt its marketing, and why?
cards.back:
Mass market — a large market in which many firms sell similar products to customers with broadly the same needs.

Niche market — a small, specialised part of a larger market, with customers who want something particular, such as gluten-free bread or kit for left-handed golfers.

  • A firm in a mass market: it sells to millions of customers in many countries → it keeps one global brand but changes the recipe, pack size or adverts for each region → it fits local tastes while keeping most of its economies of scale → high sales at a low margin.
  • A firm in a niche market: its buyers want much the same thing wherever they live → little changes beyond the language → a small niche at home becomes a large market overall, sold at a high margin.

A UK maker of scuba-diving equipment sells to divers worldwide, who want the same kit wherever they dive. It needs to translate its manuals and website, and little else.

source.verbatim: a large market in which many firms sell similar products to customers with broadly the same needs.

cards.topic: 3.3 Impact of Globalisation on Global Companies
cards.front: Evaluate whether a UK firm entering a new market abroad should adapt its product and marketing to local demand-side factors.
cards.back:
For adapting: a product and marketing that suit local culture, tastes and language → more customers buy it, and fewer are put off or offended → higher sales, and less risk of a costly relaunch or a damaged brand.

Against: research, translation and new packaging cost money. In a small market, selling the standard product may earn more profit.

It depends on:

  • How different the market is: a country where English is widely spoken and tastes are similar to the UK's needs few changes. One with a different language and very different tastes needs far more.
  • Mass or niche: a mass-market firm usually changes the recipe, pack or adverts for each region. A niche firm's buyers want much the same thing everywhere, so it may change little beyond the language.

Judgement: adapting pays where the market is large and its customers differ a lot from UK customers, so the extra sales are likely to cover the cost. In a small market close to the UK's, the standard product may earn more.

In the exam, name the factor, then finish the chain: what the difference does to sales, how the firm adapts, and what adapting costs. Then judge whether the extra sales are likely to cover that cost.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Define a host country and a home country. Why does an exam answer on a multinational need to say who gains and who loses?
cards.back:
Host country — a country an MNC sets up in. Its home country is where its head office is.

A multinational corporation (MNC) is a business with operations, such as factories, offices or shops, in more than one country.

An MNC brings money, jobs and new methods to a host country, but it can also squeeze out local firms and send its profits home. The same factory can help one group and harm another, so name the group affected, finish the chain, and judge which effect is largest.

A car maker with its head office in Japan opens a factory in the UK: Japan is the home country and the UK is the host country.

source.verbatim: a country an MNC sets up in. Its home country is where its head office is.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning: how can a large MNC site affect the local economy around it? Cover jobs, wages, local suppliers, local competitors and the community. What decides how much the area gains?
cards.back:
• Jobs: the site hires local people → unemployment in the area falls → the new workers spend more in local shops → jobs are created in businesses that never deal with the MNC.
  • Wages: the MNC pays more than local employers to attract staff → local firms raise pay to keep theirs → wages across the area rise.
  • Local suppliers: the MNC buys parts, food, cleaning and transport nearby → local firms win contracts → their sales and profits rise, and they hire too.
  • Local competitors: the MNC has economies of scale and a known brand → it undercuts small local rivals → they lose sales, and some close with the loss of their jobs.
  • Community and environment: more lorries, noise and pollution → air and water quality fall → residents' health and quality of life suffer.

How much the area gains depends on:

  • Where it buys its inputs: an MNC that imports most of its parts gives local suppliers little.
  • The jobs it creates: low-skilled assembly work raises incomes less than skilled jobs, especially if the senior posts go to staff from the home country.
  • Local laws: where rules on pay, safety and pollution are weak or poorly enforced, workers and residents are more likely to lose out.

A food-processing plant that buys its vegetables from nearby farms spreads far more of its spending locally than an assembly plant that ships in every part.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Evaluate whether an MNC benefits the national economy of its host country. Consider the balance of payments, skills, consumers, business culture and tax revenues.
cards.back:
Benefits:

  • Balance of payments: exports from the new site earn foreign currency, and goods once imported are made at home.
  • Technology and skills: workers learn new methods, and local suppliers copy them.
  • Consumers: more choice, and lower prices from economies of scale.
  • Business culture: new management methods, such as lean production, spread to local firms.
  • Tax revenues: corporation tax on the MNC's profits, plus income tax paid by the new workers.

Costs:

  • Balance of payments: imported parts, and profits sent to the home country, are outflows on the current account.
  • Technology and skills: research and skilled jobs often stay in the home country.
  • Consumers: if local rivals close, choice falls and the MNC can raise prices.
  • Business culture: practices that clash with local customs, such as long hours or refusing to deal with trade unions.
  • Tax revenues: tax breaks offered to attract the MNC, and profit moved abroad by transfer pricing, cut what it pays.

It depends on:

  • The deal it struck: a government that offers large grants or tax breaks to win an MNC gets less back in tax.
  • Where profits go: profit reinvested in the host country keeps adding to growth. Profit sent home does not.
  • The size of the economy: in a small, developing economy, one large MNC can dominate whole industries and gain power over the government.

Judgement: the host country gains most when the MNC buys locally, reinvests its profits and pays tax on them. It gains least when it gave large tax breaks to win a site that imports its parts and sends its profits home.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Define transfer pricing. How can an MNC use it to pay less tax, and who loses when it does?
cards.back:
Transfer pricing — the prices one part of an MNC charges another part, in a different country, for goods, services or the use of its brand.

Tax rates on profit differ between countries → the MNC sets its internal prices to report less profit where tax is high and more where it is low → it pays less tax in total.

  • The government: less profit reported → less corporation tax collected → less to spend on schools and roads, or other taxes must rise.
  • Domestic firms: the MNC pays a lower tax rate on the same profit → it keeps more to cut prices or invest → local rivals compete at a disadvantage.

Transfer pricing is legal if the prices are close to what two independent firms would charge each other. Tax authorities challenge prices set to move profit, but that is hard to prove for a brand name, which has no market price.

source.verbatim: the prices one part of an MNC charges another part, in a different country, for goods, services or the use of its brand.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front:
An MNC's chain of gyms in a high-tax country makes £20 million profit a year, taxed there at 30%. A sister company in a low-tax country, where profit is taxed at 10%, starts charging the gym chain £8 million a year for the use of the brand.

(a) Calculate the gym chain's profit after the charge. (b) Calculate the MNC's total tax bill before and after the charge. (c) How much corporation tax does the high-tax country lose?
cards.back:
(a) Profit in the high-tax country: £20m − £8m = £12 million. The £8 million is now profit of the sister company.

(b) Total tax bill:

  • Before: £20m × 30% = £6 million.
  • After: £12m × 30% = £3.6m in the high-tax country, plus £8m × 10% = £0.8m in the low-tax country = £4.4 million.

The MNC saves £6m − £4.4m = £1.6 million a year.

(c) Tax lost by the high-tax country: £6m − £3.6m = £2.4 million a year.

The MNC still makes £20 million in total. Only the country where the profit is reported has changed. Whether £8 million is a fair price for the brand is hard for the tax authority to prove, because a brand name has no market price.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Define business ethics. Why do MNCs face more ethical choices than most firms?
cards.back:
Business ethics — the moral principles that guide a firm's decisions, about what is right as well as what is legal or profitable.

MNCs work in countries where laws on pay, safety and pollution are weaker than at home → something banned in the UK may be legal elsewhere → the firm has to decide for itself what is right, not just what is allowed.

Acting ethically usually costs more, so there is often a trade-off with profit.

Legal does not mean ethical. An MNC paying the local minimum wage for very long working weeks may break no law. Judge the firm against what it could afford and what its customers expect, as well as against the law.

source.verbatim: the moral principles that guide a firm's decisions, about what is right as well as what is legal or profitable.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Build the chains of reasoning for three stakeholder conflicts an MNC faces. Who bears the cost in each?
cards.back:
An MNC's stakeholders are spread across many countries, and their aims often clash.

  • Shareholders and overseas workers: shareholders want higher profit → the MNC holds factory pay down → lower costs and bigger dividends, but workers stay poorly paid.
  • Customers and suppliers' workers: customers in high-income countries want low prices → the MNC pushes its suppliers to cut costs → suppliers cut wages or skimp on safety.
  • The MNC and the host community: a factory draws heavily on local water → less is left for farms and homes → the firm's costs stay low while local people bear the cost.

A clothing retailer that promises ever-lower prices to shoppers at home may be squeezing the wages of the workers who make its clothes.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Define a living wage. Is it fair for an MNC to pay low wages in a developing country? Give both views, and the effect of raising pay.
cards.back:
Living wage — the pay a worker needs to cover basic needs, such as food, housing and healthcare, where they live.

Whether the pay is fair is an ethical judgement:

  • A fair deal: MNCs often pay more than local firms or farm work → workers are better off than they would be without the job.
  • Exploitation: pay is below a living wage → workers need long hours or a second job to get by → the MNC keeps its costs low at their expense.

Working conditions raise the same questions: long hours, unpaid overtime, unsafe buildings and machinery, and bans on joining a trade union.

Raising pay and standards → higher unit costs → higher prices or lower profit. Better-paid, safer staff tend to stay longer and work harder, which wins back some of that cost.

source.verbatim: the pay a worker needs to cover basic needs, such as food, housing and healthcare, where they live.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Explain the ethical issues an MNC faces over the environment, its supply chain and its marketing. Build a chain for each.
cards.back:
Environment. Cleaner production costs money, and the damage from pollution falls on people outside the firm, an external cost.

  • Emissions: cheap, dirty fuel and no filters → lower energy and equipment costs → smoke harms local health, and greenhouse gases add to climate change.
  • Waste disposal: chemicals or plastic are dumped instead of treated → disposal costs fall → water and soil are poisoned for the farms and families nearby.

Supply chain. The people making a product may be several steps away from the firm that sells it, so problems are hard to see from head office.

  • Exploitation of labour: suppliers under pressure on price pay below the legal minimum, force unpaid overtime or keep workers' passports. At worst this is forced labour.
  • Child labour: children work instead of going to school, often producing raw materials such as cotton or cocoa far down the chain.

A brand that does not own the factory still has its name tied to what happens there.

Marketing.

  • Misleading product labelling: a label claims a product is "natural" or healthier than it is → customers buy it on a false belief → sales rise at first, but the firm risks fines and lost trust when found out. False green claims are greenwashing.
  • Inappropriate promotional activities: promotion aimed at people the product could harm, such as sugary snacks advertised to young children → higher sales → harm to those buyers → complaints, boycotts and tighter rules.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Evaluate whether acting ethically raises or lowers an MNC's profit.
cards.back:
Lowers profit: better pay, cleaner production and supplier checks → higher unit costs → higher prices or lower profit, and a disadvantage against rivals who cut corners.

Raises profit:

  • Higher sales: a good reputation → customers who care choose the brand, and some pay more for it → higher sales and margins.
  • Lower risk: fewer scandals → less chance of boycotts, fines and lost contracts → steadier profit over time.

It depends on:

  • How visible the brand is: a scandal hurts a well-known consumer brand far more than a firm that sells parts to other businesses.
  • Price elasticity of demand: where demand is price elastic, as for cheap clothing, buyers switch to rivals if prices rise, so ethical costs are hard to pass on.
  • The time period: ethical choices cost money now, while the gains in reputation and staff loyalty build up over years.

Judgement: in the short run, acting ethically usually costs profit. Over time it is most likely to pay for a well-known consumer brand whose customers care, and least likely for a firm selling cheap goods to price-sensitive buyers, or parts to other businesses.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Why are MNCs hard to control? Build the chains for their political influence: lobbying and the threat to leave.
cards.back:
An MNC operates in many countries, so no one government's laws cover everything it does. Governments also compete for MNC investment, and an MNC that dislikes one country's rules can move its factory, or its profits, somewhere else.

  • Lobbying: the MNC pays lobbyists and meets ministers to argue its case → the government hears mostly the MNC's side → it agrees more lenient tax rules or weaker regulation.
  • The threat to leave: the MNC says it will invest elsewhere → the government fears losing jobs and tax → it offers tax breaks or delays tougher rules.

Governments can still push back, especially when the public is on their side: a firm questioned in public over how little tax it pays may face a backlash from customers, and change course to protect its sales.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Explain how legal control and social media can change an MNC's behaviour. Give the limits of each.
cards.back:
Legal control: laws set the minimum standard on pay, health and safety, pollution, competition and tax → an MNC that breaks them faces fines, and in the worst cases criminal charges. A home country can also reach supply chains abroad: under the UK's Modern Slavery Act 2015, large firms doing business in the UK must publish a statement each year on what they are doing to stop slavery in their business and supply chains.

Limits: laws only work if they are enforced. Some host countries lack the inspectors and courts to do it, and MNCs can afford lawyers to find loopholes. The Modern Slavery Act requires a statement but not action, so a firm can report that it has done little.

Social media: anyone can share evidence, such as a worker's video from a factory floor → the post spreads worldwide within hours → the MNC's reputation suffers in every market → it has to respond quickly to protect sales.

Limits: stories fade within days, false claims spread as fast as true ones, and many people who share a post keep buying the product.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Define a pressure group. How can one change an MNC's behaviour, and what limits its power?
cards.back:
Pressure group — an organisation that campaigns to change the behaviour of businesses or governments, such as Greenpeace on the environment or Amnesty International on human rights.

A campaign exposes poor practice through reports, protests or a call to boycott → bad publicity and lost sales → the MNC changes its practice to protect its brand.

The limits: most groups have small budgets beside an MNC's, and a boycott works only if enough customers join it.

A boycott can hurt a famous brand that sells to the public. It does little to a firm that sells steel to car makers, where the law matters more.

source.verbatim: an organisation that campaigns to change the behaviour of businesses or governments, such as Greenpeace on the environment or Amnesty International on human rights.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Define self-regulation. Give ways an MNC, or a whole industry, can regulate itself.
cards.back:
Self-regulation — when a firm or industry sets and checks its own standards of behaviour, without the law requiring it.

An MNC might:

  • make every supplier sign a code of conduct
  • audit its suppliers' factories
  • publish its emissions each year
  • sign up to a voluntary international code, such as the UN Global Compact.

A whole industry: UK advertisers wrote their own rules, and pay for the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) to enforce them through a levy on advertising spend.

source.verbatim: when a firm or industry sets and checks its own standards of behaviour, without the law requiring it.

cards.topic: 3.4 Impact of Globalisation on Local and National Economies
cards.front: Evaluate whether self-regulation can control an MNC's behaviour as well as outside control by governments, campaigners and customers.
cards.back:
For self-regulation:

  • It is cheaper for taxpayers, and quicker to change than a law.
  • Firms know their own industry and supply chains best.
  • A firm can go beyond the law and win customers who care.

Against:

  • There are no legal penalties, so a firm can ignore its own code.
  • A firm writing its own rules may set standards it finds easy to meet.
  • Codes can be publicity with no real change behind them.

But outside control has limits too. It depends on:

  • Bargaining power: the rules of a large market such as the US or EU carry weight, because MNCs need access to it. A poorer country that badly needs the jobs and investment is unlikely to push hard.
  • Whether countries act together: an MNC can avoid one country's rules by moving elsewhere. Rules agreed by many countries are harder to escape.
  • The type of firm: boycotts and social media work on a famous consumer brand. For a firm whose customers are other businesses, the law matters more.

Judgement: self-regulation works best where laws and outside pressure remain in the background, giving firms a reason to keep to their codes. Without them, nothing stops a firm ignoring its own code.

cards.front: Define the labour force. Give three reasons the global labour force has grown.
cards.back:
Labour force — everyone of working age who is either in work or actively looking for it.

The global labour force has grown by more than a billion people since 1991. The main reasons:

  • Population growth: most of the extra workers are in developing countries, especially in South Asia and Africa, where populations are young and still growing.
  • More women in paid work: in many countries, including the UK, better education and changing attitudes have brought more women into the labour force.
  • Economies opening up: as China, India and the former Soviet bloc joined world trade, hundreds of millions of workers came within reach of global firms.

source.verbatim: everyone of working age who is either in work or actively looking for it.

cards.front: Define structural change. Name the four sectors of an economy, with an example of each. How do jobs move between them as an economy develops?
cards.back:
Structural change — a long-term shift in the share of jobs and output between the sectors of an economy.

  • Primary: extracts raw materials and grows food, such as farming, fishing and mining.
  • Secondary: turns raw materials into goods, such as manufacturing and construction.
  • Tertiary: provides services, such as retail, hospitality, transport and health care.
  • Quaternary: provides knowledge-based services, such as research and development, IT and consultancy.

As an economy develops, jobs move from the primary sector to the secondary, then to the tertiary and quaternary sectors. Many developing countries are still moving workers off farms and into factories, where each worker produces far more, so incomes rise. The UK made that move long ago and has since shifted from manufacturing to services.

source.verbatim: a long-term shift in the share of jobs and output between the sectors of an economy.

cards.front: Why do jobs move between sectors? Build the chains for what happens when an industry declines, and say what decides how costly the change is.
cards.back:
Jobs move between sectors because of:

  • Rising incomes: people spend a bigger share on services such as eating out, travel and health care.
  • Higher productivity: machines let farms and factories produce more with fewer workers, so jobs there fall even when output does not.
  • Global competition: much manufacturing has moved to lower-cost countries, especially in Asia.
  • Technology: new industries, such as software and online services, create jobs in the quaternary sector.

When an industry declines:

  • Its workers: plants close → their skills or location don't match the new jobs → structural unemployment → lower incomes, sometimes for years.
  • The local area: a large employer closes → its former staff spend less in local shops → more firms cut jobs, and whole towns can decline.
  • Firms in growing sectors: demand for new skills outruns supply → skill shortages → they pay more to recruit, which raises their costs.

The cost depends on: labour mobility, as workers who can retrain or move to where the jobs are find new work faster, and the speed of change, as a slow decline lets people retire or retrain while a sudden closure leaves them stranded.

cards.front: What does it mean for labour markets to be interdependent? Build the four ways globalisation links them, and say what decides how closely two are linked.
cards.back:
Labour markets are interdependent when a change in one country affects jobs and wages in another.

  • Trade: a major trading partner goes into recession → it buys fewer imports → exporters elsewhere cut output → they cut jobs.
  • Firms moving production: wages rise in one country → MNCs move factories to cheaper ones → jobs fall in the first and rise in the second. As wages in China rose, some clothing production moved to countries such as Vietnam and Bangladesh.
  • Migration: workers move to countries with higher pay or more jobs → labour supply rises where they arrive and falls where they left.
  • Digital services: work such as coding, accounting and customer service can be done online from anywhere → firms hire across borders → a programmer in the UK competes with one in India.

How closely two are linked depends on:

  • Barriers: tariffs, migration rules and work permits all slow the links.
  • Skills: the more specialised the job, the fewer people worldwide can do it, so the less its pay is held down by competition from abroad.

cards.front: Evaluate whether a growing global labour force harms workers in high-income countries such as the UK.
cards.back:
Who loses:

  • Low-skilled workers: they compete with workers abroad who cost less → jobs in industries such as textiles move overseas → job losses, or lower pay for those who stay.

Who gains:

  • Skilled workers: firms sell into bigger global markets → more demand for design, engineering and finance skills → higher wages.
  • Firms: more workers are available in low-wage countries → firms move production there or buy from suppliers there → lower costs → lower prices or higher profit.

It depends on:

  • Productivity as well as wages: a worker paid half as much who produces a third as much costs more per unit of output. A UK worker paid £18 an hour who makes 9 units costs £2 a unit. A worker abroad paid £9 an hour who makes 3 units costs £3 a unit.
  • Whether the work can move: a factory job can go abroad, but a plumber or a care worker has to be where the customer is.

Judgement: say which workers you mean. Low-skilled workers in jobs that can move abroad lose most. Skilled workers can gain, and those whose work has to be done locally are protected. An answer that names the group earns more than "workers lose out".

cards.front: Define the wage rate. Sketch how the wage is set in a competitive labour market. What makes the wage rise, and what increases the supply of labour to a job?
cards.back:
Wage rate — the price of labour, paid per hour, week or year of work.

In a competitive labour market, the wage is set where firms' demand for labour, D(L), meets workers' supply of it, S(L): the wage W1, with Q1 people employed. MRP is the extra revenue the last worker brings in, and AC is the average cost of a worker, which is the wage.

A wage rises when demand for labour rises or supply falls. The supply of labour to a job is the number of people willing and able to do it at each wage. It rises when:

  • pay in similar jobs falls
  • non-wage benefits improve, such as flexible hours, job security or a good pension
  • fewer qualifications are needed
  • the working-age population grows, through higher birth rates in the past, or migration
  • work pays more than not working, through lower income tax, cheaper childcare or less generous out-of-work benefits.

Each of these raises supply, so it lowers the wage. The reverse of each cuts supply and raises the wage.

That is why pay differs so much between jobs: few people have a surgeon's training and hospitals need surgeons badly, while almost anyone can start work in a shop.
